amendments.rule: Expect more fusion rather than new rules: *Nor* for waw plus a negative, *But* for `כִּי אִם`, *whatsoever* for `כֹּל אֲשֶׁר`. The same *Nor* may rest on a present negative in one line and a gapped one in the next; align what is actually there. **Distance does not break these fusions.** Where the ASV's single word still says what every morpheme in it says, the unit stands however far apart they stand: `וְ ... לֹא` → *Nor* across a fronted prepositional phrase or object, `לֹא ... לְעוֹלָם` → *never* across the verb it negates. This is the far side of rule 30's contiguity condition, and the difference is what the English word carries. `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded* drops the preposition's own sense, so rule 2 splits it and the preposition is `unrepresented`; *Nor* still carries both the coordination and the negation and *never* both the negation and the time, so nothing is left over to mark. Head a *Nor* on the negative, which is what distinguishes it from a bare *and*. A *never* is a genuine tie between the negative and the temporal noun — the corpus heads it both ways — so choose, and say in the note which reading you took and that the corpus heads it both ways. **A single *no* written for a `כֹּל` and a negative standing in the same clause is one of these fusions.** Where Hebrew writes `כָּל` on the noun and `לֹא`, or a prohibitive `אַל`, on its verb, and the ASV spends one word on the pair — `כָל־אָדָם לֹא־יִהְיֶה` → *there shall be* ***no*** *man*, `וְכָל־מְלָאכָה לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ` → *shall do* ***no*** *manner of work* — that word carries both the universal and the negation, exactly as *whatsoever* carries both morphemes of `כֹּל אֲשֶׁר`, so the two share one unit, discontinuous around the noun and the verb under rule 25, and headed on the negative for the reason a *Nor* is: the negation is what distinguishes *no* from *all*. Do not read rule 15's determiner sentences as a direction to give the word to one of them and mark the other `unrepresented`; that rule counts one determiner against one morpheme, and here one English word answers to two. The noun keeps its own English, including any generic the ASV supplies to expand it under rule 31, so *manner of work* is `מְלָאכָה`'s, headed on *work*. Where the ASV instead writes a word for each — a *not* on the verb beside an *any* or an *all* on the noun — nothing is indivisible, rule 2 splits them, and each morpheme takes the word written for it. **A *cannot* is not one of these fusions, because the verb's lexeme stands outside it.** Where the ASV writes *cannot* for a negated verb, the word carries the negation together with a modal English has supplied, and it goes whole to the negative while the verb keeps its subject pronoun and its lexical verb under rule 17: `לֹא יִצְעָדוּ` → *they* ***cannot*** *go* gives *cannot* to `לֹא` and *they go* to the verb, exactly as rule 48 gives such a word to the privative `מִן` that carries the negation there. The corpus aligns `לֹא` alone to *cannot*, headed on it, in fourteen units. **But where `יָכֹל` stands in the clause, that verb is what the modal renders**, and the two morphemes share the one indivisible word — `לֹא אוּכַל` → *I cannot*, `לֹא יוּכְלוּ` → *they cannot*, `לֹא נוּכַל` → *we cannot* — headed on *cannot*, which is how the corpus reads all eleven of those units. And where the ASV writes the negation and the modal as two words instead — *are not able*, *shall not be able* — nothing is indivisible, rule 2 splits them, the negative takes only its own *not*, and the rest belongs to the verb, its complement headed by rule 44. Read the English the ASV wrote and the verb the Hebrew wrote, not the modality the Hebrew implies.
amendments.why: LEV.16.17 and 16.29 both hand a single *no* to a כֹּל and a לֹא standing in one clause, and no rule decided it. Rule 15 counts determiners one against one morpheme and offers two candidates here, so a pass reading it alone could give the word to either and mark the other unrepresented — three possible outcomes for a construction that recurs through the priestly law. Rule 35 is the right home because it already fuses כֹּל with a neighbouring morpheme (*whatsoever* for כֹּל אֲשֶׁר), already licenses fusion across intervening material, and already fixes the head on the negative for the same reason. The corpus supports the shape rather than contradicting it: it fuses כָּל הָ into *whosoever* in eight aligned and six noncompositional units. The amendment also names the split case so the rule cannot be read as forcing a fusion the ASV did not write.

conventions: כָּל on a noun and a negative on its verb, rendered by a single *no*, share one discontinuous unit headed on the negative: כָל־אָדָם לֹא־יִהְיֶה → *there shall be no man* (16.17) and וְכָל־מְלָאכָה לֹא תַעֲשׂוּ → *shall do no manner of work* (16.29). The noun keeps its own English, including the supplied *manner of* that expands it under rule 31. Neither morpheme is marked unrepresented beside the other.

The appositional לְ of לְכָל־חַטֹּאתָם takes the ASV's *even* (16.16, 16.21), since it is the morpheme standing on the phrase that word introduces. Where the ASV writes *even* before an appositive on which no marker and no preposition stands, the word is `added` (16.32, בִּגְדֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ, the clause's one marker standing on אֶת־בִּגְדֵי הַבָּד). Count the ASV's *even*s against the morphemes standing on the appositive rather than against the markers elsewhere in the clause.

The English *make atonement* reaches its object through *for*, and that word goes to whichever morpheme stands on the object: an אֵת marker takes it (16.20 once, 16.33 three times) and the markers for which the ASV writes no second *for* stay unrepresented (16.20 twice); an עַל or בַּעַד standing there takes it instead (16.6, 16.11, 16.16, 16.17, 16.24, 16.30, 16.33, 16.34). Count the ASV's *for*s against the marked objects, one per marker.

In אֶל־מִבֵּית לַפָּרֹכֶת (16.2, 16.12, 16.15) and אֶל־מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה (16.27) the מִן and its construct noun fuse to the single word *within* / *without* under rule 30, and both the governing אֶל and the following לְ are unrepresented under rule 40, because the one English word states the whole relation. This accounts for eight of the chapter's BSB status disagreements.

Where the nomen rectum is rendered as a prenominal attributive under rule 28 — הַבָּד → *linen*, הַקֹּדֶשׁ → *holy* — the article on that rectum takes the phrase's single written *the* and the construct noun takes none: בִּגְדֵי הַבָּד → *the linen garments* (16.23, 16.32), בִּגְדֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ → *the holy garments* (16.32), מִקְדַּשׁ הַקֹּדֶשׁ → *the holy sanctuary* (16.33). This is rule 29's anarthrous-rectum fronting, and it is what distinguishes those phrases from כְּתֹנֶת בַּד קֹדֶשׁ → *the holy linen coat* (16.4), where no article morpheme stands and the construct takes a supplied *the*.

report: Checked all 58 candidate lemma groups and, because the table is keyed by source lemma and so blind to `added` units, read the 34-verse dump end to end as well. No cross-verse split found; patches is empty.

The supplied object pronouns are what the table could not show, and they are consistent: *it* / *him* is `added` at 16.12, 16.14, 16.18 and 16.21, where the Hebrew verb carries no object morpheme, and aligned to the suffix at 16.10, 16.15 and 16.19, where one stands. Rule 44 applied the same way in every place.

The *even* group is not a split. 16.16 and 16.21 have a לְ standing on the appositive itself and give it the word; 16.32 writes *even* before a phrase on which neither a marker nor a preposition stands, the clause's one marker being on אֶת־בִּגְדֵי הַבָּד, so it is `added` under rule 16's own limit. The two readings are one count, not two analyses.

שָׁלַח heads on *send* at 16.10 and 16.21 (*send away*, a phrasal particle) and on *go* at 16.22 and 16.26 (*let go*, a light verb plus complement). Rule 44's subtraction gives opposite answers for those two English renderings, so the difference is licensed. The אֵת markers behave the same way: the ASV writes one *for* in 16.20 and three in 16.33, and the chapter counted them, leaving the rest unrepresented.

Article counting is uniform across the chapter: one written *the* goes to the present article with the agreement article unrepresented (16.20, 16.21, 16.23, 16.29, 16.32, 16.33), two written *the*s give one to the article and a supplied one to the construct (16.6, 16.11, 16.13-16.15, 16.18, 16.21, 16.24, 16.25, 16.27), and no written *the* leaves the article unrepresented (16.12, 16.30, and *in water* at 16.4, 16.24, 16.26, 16.28).

BSB: 25 status disagreements, and none is a genuine error. Nine object markers and the four לְ of מִבֵּית/מִחוּץ לַ־ are the documented convention difference; the five articles are rule 47 agreement articles, the demonstrative phrase of 16.30 and the *a censer* of 16.12; the four R are the אֶל and the resultative לְ that the ASV's recasting leaves nothing to say; the two Sp3ms are the resumptive suffix of *upon which*, which the ASV writes in two words rather than as *whereon*; and the 16.20 waw opens an apodosis for which the ASV writes no connective. Nothing was changed to improve the rate.

Five conventions recorded. The report counts 107 repeated notes against 0 conventions, but most of those repeats restate rules the contract already binds every verse with; the five logged are the judgments a later reader would otherwise have to rediscover.

One amendment, to rule 35: כָּל plus a negative rendered by a single *no* (16.17, 16.29) hands one English word to two morphemes, which rule 15's determiner counting does not settle and rule 35's fusion list did not yet name.

Not promoted, and recorded here instead: 16.27 fuses אֲשֶׁר with the resumptive suffix of דָּמָם into *whose*, on the pattern rule 22 records for *wherein*. The corpus aligns a bare suffix to *whose* in 72 units but nothing in the precedent shows how an אֲשֶׁר standing beside such a suffix is handled, so the reading stands as the verse pass took it and no rule is written on it.
Two head choices remain genuine ties and carry their competing reading in the verse note, as rule 8 requires: *solemn rest* at 16.31 (headed on *rest*) and *home born* at 16.29 (headed on *home*).
